title: Making Server-Side API Requests with Axios
summary: Shows how an Express server can call a third-party API itself, first with Node's built-in https module (verbose) and then with the Axios package (one line). The exercise builds an 'I'm Bored' site that fetches a random activity, filters by type and participants via query parameters, and handles 404 errors.

concepts.heading: Why the server makes requests
points: Besides browsers and Postman, a Node/Express backend often needs to call another company's public API and use the response, e.g. to render a page.
Flow: your server sends a request to the provider's server, which replies with the data; your server then passes it to the template.

concepts.heading: The native way: https module
points: https ships with Node, no install needed.
Configure an options object: the host/base URL, the path (endpoint) and the HTTP method.
Call https.request(options, callback). The response arrives as a stream of chunks, so you append each chunk to a string on the 'data' event.
On the 'end' event all chunks are in; run JSON.parse on the accumulated string to get an object, then pass it to the view.
Wrap parsing in try/catch, add an 'error' listener on the request for network failures, and call req.end() to actually send it.
Conclusion: it works but takes many lines of boilerplate.

concepts.heading: Axios
points: Axios is an npm package that simplifies server-to-server (and browser) HTTP calls, much as Express simplifies Node's raw server code. It has tens of millions of weekly downloads, used as a popularity signal when choosing packages.
axios.get(url) takes the full URL (same as you would type in a browser) and returns a promise. Use .then/.catch or async/await.
response.data holds the body; when the API returns JSON, Axios has already parsed it into a JS object, so no JSON.parse is needed.
Errors (network failure or non-2xx status) reject the promise, so one try/catch handles them all in one place.
It has aliases for the common verbs: axios.get, .post, .put, .patch, .delete.
Install with npm i axios and import it: import axios from "axios".

concepts.heading: I'm Bored exercise: how it works
points: Dependencies: axios, body-parser, ejs, express. API: bored-api.appbrewery.com with /random (one activity) and /filter (array of activities matching optional type and participants queries).
GET /: await axios.get on /random, then render the page with data = response.data. Fields shown: activity, type, participants.
POST /: the form has two selects named type and participants, so req.body.type and req.body.participants arrive as strings; empty string means 'any' (the API treats empty queries as no filter).
Build the filter URL with a template literal: /filter?type=${type}&participants=${participants}.
/filter returns an array, but the page shows one card, so pick a random element: result[Math.floor(Math.random() * result.length)].
No match makes the API answer 404, Axios rejects, and the catch block renders the page with a friendly error string.
In EJS use locals.data and locals.error to test whether each was passed; show the card when data exists, the error div when error exists.

task.name: I'm Bored activity finder
task.starting_point: Folder with index.js, views/index.ejs, public styles, solution.js and solution.ejs; dependencies axios, body-parser, ejs, express. Run npm install, then nodemon solution.js to see the finished site.
task.goal: Home page shows a random activity card; the form filters by type and participants and shows a random match; unmatched filters show 'No activities that match your criteria.'
steps: npm install, run nodemon solution.js and try the finished site (random card, education + 1 person works, education + 2 people errors).
GET /: use axios.get on the /random endpoint inside an async handler; log response.data to learn its shape.
In index.ejs output the activity, type and participants from the passed data object, and add a block for an error message.
POST /: console.log(req.body) to see type and participants.
Request /filter with both values as query parameters via axios.get and a template literal.
Pick one random item from the returned array and render index.ejs with it.
In catch, log error.message and render with a user-facing 'No activities that match your criteria.' message (optionally branch on a 404 status for more specific messages).
task.expected_result: A card with title, type and participants appears on load; Go with a valid combination shows a random matching card; an impossible combination shows the error text and the server logs a 404.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 28 - Aplication Programming Interfaces (APIs)/28.04 - Making Server-Side API Requests with Axios

pitfalls: Forgetting async/await: response would be a pending Promise and response.data undefined.
Using only .data of the response: the top-level Axios response object also has status, headers, etc.
/filter returns an array, so rendering it directly will not fit a single-card template; choose one element.
Any catch is treated as 'no matches' in the reference; network outages would show the same message. Check error.response?.status === 404 to distinguish (Extra).

In the reference repo the starter index.js already contains the finished logic and its catch renders solution.ejs; it diverges from a true blank starter. The author field in package.json is the repo owner's, ignore it.
(Extra) Build query strings with axios params ({ params: { type, participants } }) to get automatic URL encoding.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Server-side requests with Axios' (blurb: your Express server calls another API and renders the result).

Tasks: (1) axios.get a random endpoint and log response.data; (2) render fields in EJS; (3) POST handler building a filtered URL from form values; (4) choose a random array element; (5) catch errors and show a friendly message depending on error.response?.status.
Starter code: Express app with an empty async route and a form with two selects.

Interactive demo: a simulated 'API' with a fake latency and a toggle to force a 404; show the request line, status, response.data and the rendered card side by side, comparing https-module code vs Axios code line counts.
